Migrating from fftwtools

Source: vignettes/migrating-from-fftwtools.Rmd
migrating-from-fftwtools.Rmd

zufft computes the same transforms as fftwtools without the FFTW system library, and under a permissive licence. This vignette maps every fftwtools call to its zufft equivalent. Where fftwtools is installed, each example also checks that both give the same values.

library(zufft)

Two conventions to know

Scaling. fftwtools, like stats::fft(), never scales: an inverse after a forward transform multiplies by the length. zufft follows scipy.fft and divides the inverse by the length by default (norm = "backward"). Use norm = "none" to get fftwtools’ numbers exactly.

x <- c(1, 4, 2, 8, 5, 7)
fft_c2c(fft_c2c(x), inverse = TRUE)                 # x again
#> [1] 1+0i 4+0i 2+0i 8+0i 5+0i 7+0i
fft_c2c(fft_c2c(x), inverse = TRUE, norm = "none")  # 6 * x, as fftwtools
#> [1]  6+0i 24+0i 12+0i 48+0i 30+0i 42+0i

Half spectra. fftwtools’ HermConj = 1 (its default) returns the full spectrum of real input, and HermConj = 0 the non-redundant half. In zufft that is the choice between fft_c2c() and fft_r2c().

fft_c2c(x)  # full spectrum, as fftw(x) and fftw_r2c(x)
#> [1]  27+0.000000i  -5+5.196152i   0+0.000000i -11+0.000000i   0+0.000000i
#> [6]  -5-5.196152i
fft_r2c(x)  # first n %/% 2 + 1 values, as fftw_r2c(x, HermConj = 0)
#> [1]  27+0.000000i  -5+5.196152i   0+0.000000i -11+0.000000i

To go back from a half spectrum you need the original length, because an even and an odd length give the same half size. Both packages take it as n:

X <- fft_r2c(1:7)
fft_c2r(X, n = 7, norm = "none")   # as fftw_c2r(X, HermConj = 0, n = 7)
#> [1]  7 14 21 28 35 42 49

One-dimensional transforms

fftwtools zufft
fftw(x) fft_c2c(x)
fftw(x, inverse = 1) fft_c2c(x, inverse = TRUE, norm = "none")
fftw(x, HermConj = 0) (real x) fft_r2c(x)
fftw(X, inverse = 1, HermConj = 0, n = n) fft_c2r(X, n = n, norm = "none")
fftw_r2c(x) fft_c2c(x)
fftw_r2c(x, HermConj = 0) fft_r2c(x)
fftw_c2r(X, HermConj = 0, n = n) fft_c2r(X, n = n, norm = "none")
fftw_c2r(X) (full spectrum) Re(fft_c2c(X, inverse = TRUE, norm = "none"))
fftw_c2c(x, inverse = i) fft_c2c(x, inverse = i, norm = "none")

inverse = 0 and inverse = 1 work in zufft too.

z <- complex(real = rnorm(8), imaginary = rnorm(8))
all.equal(fft_c2c(z, inverse = 1, norm = "none"), fftwtools::fftw_c2c(z, inverse = 1))
#> [1] TRUE
all.equal(fft_r2c(x), fftwtools::fftw_r2c(x, HermConj = 0))
#> [1] TRUE
all.equal(fft_c2r(X, n = 7, norm = "none"), fftwtools::fftw_c2r(X, HermConj = 0, n = 7))
#> [1] TRUE

Columns of a matrix

fftwtools’ mvfftw* functions transform each column. In zufft that is axes = 1.

fftwtools zufft
mvfftw(m), mvfftw_c2c(m) fft_c2c(m, axes = 1)
mvfftw_r2c(m, HermConj = 0) fft_r2c(m, axes = 1)
mvfftw_c2r(M, HermConj = 0, n = n) fft_c2r(M, n = n, axes = 1, norm = "none")
mvfftw(..., fftplanopt = 1) nothing to do: zufft caches its plans 
m <- matrix(rnorm(24), 6)
all.equal(fft_c2c(m, axes = 1), fftwtools::mvfftw(m))
#> [1] TRUE
M <- fft_r2c(m, axes = 1)
all.equal(fft_c2r(M, n = 6, axes = 1, norm = "none"), fftwtools::mvfftw_c2r(M, HermConj = 0, n = 6))
#> [1] TRUE

Two, three and more dimensions

fftwtools zufft
fftw2d(x), fftw_c2c_2d(x), fftw3d(x), fftw_c2c_3d(x), fftw_c2c_xd(x) fft_c2c(x)
fftw_r2c_2d(x, HermConj = 0) fft_r2c(x, axes = 2:1)
fftw_r2c_3d(x, HermConj = 0) fft_r2c(x, axes = 3:1)

FFTW stores arrays row by row, so fftwtools’ real 2-D and 3-D transforms halve R’s first dimension. zufft halves the last axis you list, so list the first axis last. That is also the faster order in R, where the first axis is the contiguous one.

x2 <- matrix(rnorm(35), 5, 7)
all.equal(fft_r2c(x2, axes = 2:1), fftwtools::fftw_r2c_2d(x2, HermConj = 0))
#> [1] TRUE
all.equal(fft_c2c(x2), fftwtools::fftw2d(x2))
#> [1] TRUE

What you gain

  • No system library. zufft compiles its bundled ducc0 code, so install.packages("zufft") is enough, everywhere.
  • No GPL. zufft is MIT-licensed and its bundled code BSD-3, so a package that imports it keeps its own licence.
  • Speed. On the benchmark grid in the package’s bench/RESULTS.md, zufft is faster than fftwtools on most cases and within 1.5 times everywhere, because it caches its plans while fftwtools plans on every call. Multi-dimensional complex transforms gain the most.
  • Threads. workers = 2 (or fft_workers(2)) splits a transform over threads; fftwtools has none.
  • More transforms. fft_dct() and fft_dst() (types 1 to 4), any subset of axes, cropping and zero-padding with n, and fft_next_len() for fast lengths.
  • Untouched inputs. fft_c2r() never modifies its input, while FFTW’s complex-to-real transform destroys it.
